ai-at-work.title: Salesforce rolls out new Slackbot AI agent as it battles Microsoft and Google in workplace AI
ai-at-work.excerpt: Salesforce on Tuesday launched an entirely rebuilt version of Slackbot, the company's workplace assistant, transforming it from a simple notification tool into what executives describe as a fully powe
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Salesforce rebuilt Slackbot from a basic notification tool into a full AI agent that can search data, draft documents, and execute tasks for employees. This matters because workplace AI assistants are becoming table stakes, and how well they integrate with your actual work determines whether people use them or ignore them. The real test isn't the flashy demo in the earnings call, it's whether your Slack users will actually trust it to do something without checking their work first.

ai-at-work.title: Radware adds Claude Code protection and compliance reporting to agent security
ai-at-work.excerpt: Application and network security company Radware Ltd. today expanded its Agentic AI Protection product with compliance reporting, deeper visibility into artificial intelligence agent activity, and new
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Radware beefed up its AI agent security platform with better compliance reporting, visibility into agent behavior, and specific protection for Claude Code running on developer machines. This matters because enterprises are actually deploying AI agents into production now, which means security teams need real tools instead of theoretical frameworks. Honestly, it's refreshing to see vendors shipping practical features for problems that actually exist rather than solving for AI scenarios that exist only in PowerPoint decks.

ai-at-work.title: IBM debuts compact z17 mainframes and LinuxONE servers for on-premises enterprise AI
ai-at-work.excerpt: IBM Corp. today announced a massive expansion of its on-premises enterprise infrastructure lineup, with new single-frame and rack-mount versions of its iconic z17 mainframes and more compact LinuxONE
ai-at-work.dwp_take: IBM just rolled out smaller, more affordable versions of its mainframes and Linux servers so enterprises can run AI workloads on their own hardware instead of renting cloud capacity. This matters because it gives organizations real options for keeping sensitive data in-house while handling compute-heavy AI tasks, which beats the cloud-only religion some vendors preach. Look, mainframes aren't sexy, but they're reliable workhorses that enterprises actually trust with their money, so IBM smartly making them more accessible for AI is honestly good news for companies tired of cloud lock-in.

ai-at-work.title: Syntiant, which makes low-power chips for on-device AI, files for initial public offering
ai-at-work.excerpt: A chipmaker called Syntiant Corp. that specializes in making low-powered processors that run artificial intelligence locally on devices has filed to go public. The company filed its initial public off
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Syntiant, a chipmaker focused on low-power processors that run AI directly on devices rather than in the cloud, filed for its IPO today to capitalize on investor hunger for AI plays. This matters because on-device AI means faster processing, better privacy, and reduced reliance on cloud infrastructure, which could reshape how workplace apps handle sensitive data and real-time intelligence. Finally, after three decades watching tech cycles, I'll believe the privacy benefits when I see them actually implemented instead of just marketed.

tools-tech.title: Adobe premieres a second Patch Tuesday each month to deliver fixes faster
tools-tech.excerpt: Adobe will now issue security patches for its products twice as often to deal with the increasing pace of software vulnerability discovery and exploitation. This follows Oracle’s decision to increase
tools-tech.dwp_take: Adobe is adding a second Patch Tuesday on the fourth of each month to speed up security fixes alongside their existing second Tuesday schedule. This matters because digital workplace managers already juggle multiple vendor patch calendars, and adding more patch days means more testing cycles and deployment windows to manage across your organization. Look, I get why vendors need to move faster on security, but this is going to turn your IT team's calendar into a patchwork quilt that nobody asked for.

industry-news.title: Singapore’s Shift to Passkeys Reveals a Password Problem
industry-news.excerpt: Singapore's rollout of passkeys for Singpass signals a critical shift in digital identity. This article explores how device-bound authentication, such as Windows Hello for Business, helps Singaporean
industry-news.dwp_take: Singapore is rolling out passkeys through Singpass, moving away from traditional passwords toward device-bound authentication like Windows Hello for Business. This matters because most organizations still rely on passwords that employees reuse, forget, and share, making them a constant security headache for anyone managing digital workplaces. Honestly, it's refreshing to see a government actually doing something about passwords instead of just asking people to use more exclamation marks and numbers, which has never worked on anyone except the IT person writing the policy.

industry-news.title: The hidden cost of AI support: Why MSPs still struggle with escalation and repeated diagnosis
industry-news.excerpt: Why MSP service desks still struggle despite growing investments in AI automation
industry-news.dwp_take: Microsoft and other vendors have been selling AI-powered support tools that promise to cut costs and speed up ticket resolution, but managed service providers are finding that AI actually struggles with escalation handoffs and keeps re-diagnosing the same problems instead of learning from previous tickets. This matters because digital workplace teams rely on MSPs to keep their infrastructure running, and when support gets stuck in an AI loop doing the same troubleshooting twice, it tanks productivity and burns through those cost savings everyone promised. After three decades watching tech solve problems by creating new ones, I can tell you this is basically what happens when vendors optimize for the demo instead of the actual job.

industry-news.title: Workday expands EMEA VAR ecosystem with HR Path UK&I partnership
industry-news.excerpt: The partnership will see HR Path directly sell Workday solutions to SMBs across Scotland and Ireland
industry-news.dwp_take: Workday just handed its UK and Ireland small business market to HR Path as an official reseller partner. This matters because it signals where enterprise software vendors see actual growth potential: the overlooked SMB segment that's been stuck using spreadsheets and prayer for HR operations. Look, if Workday is betting real money that SMBs in Scotland and Ireland need proper HR software, someone finally noticed that not every company has 50,000 employees, which I suppose counts as progress in enterprise tech.
